::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The end-of-course project goal

Your team answers a predictive question with a public data set, in R and/or Python,
with a focus on reproducible and trustworthy workflows.
**By the end of the course**, your single Quarto document will have become a project with:

-   well-documented, modular scripts in R and/or Python
-   a pipeline automated with GNU Make
-   a reproducible Quarto report
-   a Docker container for the computational environment
-   a GitHub repository for collaboration and sharing
:::

## Milestone 2 summary

This milestone is about moving your project into a [container]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A container is a running copy of a Docker image: an isolated computer inside your computer, with the exact software and packages your project needs. Everyone who runs it gets the same environment, whatever their own laptop has installed."}.

- [ ] Run your project's environment in a Docker container, and **work in it from now on**
- [ ] Build the image on GitHub Actions for [Intel/AMD and ARM]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="These are the two main kinds of computer processor. Most Windows laptops and servers use Intel/AMD chips (linux/amd64), while Macs with Apple silicon (M1 and later) use ARM chips (linux/arm64). An image built for one kind runs slowly or not at all on the other, so you build for both."}, and publish it on Docker Hub
- [ ] Publish your report on GitHub Pages

Your reference is [docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv),
the example project the textbook's Containers chapters build up to.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Readings for this milestone

-   [Python and R in one image](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv-renv.html): what goes in the `Dockerfile`
-   [uv in a container](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-uv.html) and [renv in a container](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-renv.html): adding a package to your image
-   [renv: declaring packages in `DESCRIPTION`](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/virtual-environments-r-renv-description.html): pinning R package versions
-   [Docker Compose](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-docker-compose.html): starting the container with one command
-   [Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html): editing code inside the container
-   [Building images for several platforms](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-platforms.html): the GitHub Actions workflow in step iii
-   [Introduction to Quarto and GitHub Pages](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html) (DSCI 521): publishing the report in part 2
:::


### 1. Put your environment in a container

1.  **Copy the files.**
    Copy the [`Dockerfile`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/Dockerfile)
    and [`docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/docker-compose.yml)
    from docker-uv-renv into the root of your repository.
    Keep the Compose service's name, `analysis-env`, so the commands below work as written.
    Then remove the language your project does not use (see below).

2.  **Check your environment files.**
    The image installs your packages from your lock files,
    so these must be in your repository and agree with each other:

    -   **Python (uv):** `pyproject.toml` with every package pinned with `==`, `uv.lock` and `.python-version`.
    -   **R (renv):** `DESCRIPTION` with every package pinned with `(== x.y.z)`, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` and `renv/`.
        `DESCRIPTION` is required, and it **must list `knitr` and `rmarkdown`**
        (Quarto needs them to run the R code in your report).

3.  **Build and publish the image with GitHub Actions.**
    Copy the **two-platform** workflow from
    [Building images for several platforms](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-platforms.html)
    into `.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml`,
    and change only its `IMAGE` line to your Docker Hub repository's name, all in lowercase.
    It builds for `linux/amd64` (Intel/AMD) and `linux/arm64` (ARM, such as Apple silicon Macs)
    and pushes one image tagged `latest` and with the commit SHA.
    One team member sets up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets, as in Individual Assignment 2 (see below).
    Check that the run succeeds and that your image's tag on Docker Hub lists **both** platforms.

4.  **Use the published image in `docker-compose.yml`.**
    Replace `build: .` with your image, pinned to the [commit-SHA tag]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="Every Git commit has a unique ID called its SHA (e.g. 1a2b3c4). Your workflow tags each image it pushes with the SHA of the commit that built it, so the tag always points to that one exact image. The latest tag, by contrast, changes every time you publish."} your workflow pushed, not `latest`
    (for example, `image: yourname/yourproject:sha-1a2b3c4`).
    Keep the ssh setup: the port `2222:22` and the mount of `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`.

5.  **Work in the container from now on**, with Positron over ssh
    ([Working in a container over ssh with Positron](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-ssh-positron.html)).
    To add a package: add it with uv or renv, commit the changed files together,
    let GitHub Actions publish a new image,
    then update the tag in `docker-compose.yml` in a pull request.

6.  **Update your `README`** so its instructions use the container (see the next section).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Removing Python or R from the `Dockerfile`

::: panel-tabset
## Python only

Delete the R packages part:

-   the `RUN echo "RENV_PATHS_LIBRARY=/opt/renv/library" ...` line
-   `COPY renv.lock .Rprofile ./`
-   `COPY renv/activate.R renv/`
-   `RUN Rscript -e "renv::restore()"`
-   `libuv1-dev` in the `apt-get install` list (only the R package fs needs it)

Your project has no `DESCRIPTION`, `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile` or `renv/`.

## R only

Delete the uv part, but keep `WORKDIR /workspace`:

-   `COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.7 /uv /uvx /usr/local/bin/`
-   `ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv`
    and the `RUN echo "UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=..."` line after it
-   `COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version ./`
-   `RUN uv sync --locked`

Your project has no `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` or `.python-version`,
and you render with `quarto render` instead of `uv run quarto render`.

## Python and R

Keep both parts.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Setting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets

One team member:

1.  Creates a **public** Docker Hub repository for the project.
2.  Creates a Docker Hub [access token](https://docs.docker.com/security/access-tokens/) with Read & Write permissions.
3.  Adds two [repository secrets](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets)
    to your GitHub repository (Settings \> Secrets and variables \> Actions \> New repository secret):
    `DOCKER_USERNAME` (the Docker Hub username)
    and `DOCKER_PASSWORD` (the access token, **not** the Docker Hub password).

The workflow runs on its own when a push changes the `Dockerfile` or a lock file.
To run it by hand: **Actions** tab \> the workflow \> **Run workflow**.
:::

#### Your `README`: how to run the analysis

Write these steps in your `README`, in this order:

1.  Make an ssh key if you don't have one: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`, pressing Enter at each question.
    (Without it, Docker makes a *folder* named `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub`,
    and ssh into the container fails until you delete that folder and make the key.)
2.  Download the image: `docker compose pull`.
3.  Render the report in the container:
    -   Python, or Python and R: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render`
    -   R only: `docker compose run --rm analysis-env quarto render`

    Add your report's path after `quarto render` if your project has no `_quarto.yml` that lists it.
4.  Work in the container: `docker compose up -d` starts it, then connect with Positron over ssh.
    `docker compose down` stops it.
5.  Update the container: add a package with your environment manager, commit and push,
    wait for GitHub Actions to publish the new image,
    then update the tag in `docker-compose.yml` and run `docker compose pull`.

::: callout-important
## 5 all-or-nothing points for your README instructions

If someone can't launch your container and run your analysis by following your instructions
**exactly as written**, you lose all 5 points.
Test them on **both Windows and Mac**.
If your team doesn't have both, ask another team to test them.
:::

### 2. Publish your report on GitHub Pages

Anyone should be able to read your report online without cloning your repository.
You publish it by hand: put a [self-contained]{.term tabindex="0" data-tip="A self-contained HTML file has everything it needs (figures, styling, scripts) packed inside the one file, instead of in separate files next to it. So it still works after you copy it somewhere else."} copy of your rendered report at `docs/index.html`.
If you already published your report in Milestone 1, switch to this setup anyway, because later milestones build on it.

1.  Make the rendered report one self-contained HTML file, in its YAML header
    (skip this if your `_quarto.yml` already sets it):

    ```yaml
    format:
      html:
        embed-resources: true
    ```

    If you have only been rendering to PDF, render to HTML as well.

2.  Render your report, then copy it into `docs/` as `index.html`, and add an empty `.nojekyll` file:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p docs
    cp <path-to-your-report>.html docs/index.html
    touch docs/.nojekyll
    ```

3.  Commit and push `docs/`.
    Check that your `.gitignore` does not ignore `docs/` or `.html` files.

4.  On GitHub.com, go to **Settings \> Pages** \> **Deploy from a branch**,
    choose the `main` branch and the `/docs` folder, and click **Save**.

5.  After a few minutes, open `https://ubc-mds-2026-27.github.io/<your-repository>/`
    and check that the whole report shows, including its figures.

6.  Put this URL in your `README` (as the link to your rendered report)
    and in the **About** section of your repository.

::: callout-important
## Keep the published report up to date

`docs/index.html` is a copy.
Each time you re-render your report, copy it into `docs/` again and push.
We grade from your `1.0.0` release, and the report on GitHub Pages should match it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Why this works

-   GitHub Pages can publish the files in a `docs/` folder on `main`, exactly as they are.
-   When someone visits your site's address, the server shows the file named `index.html`.
-   With `embed-resources: true`, the report is one HTML file that holds its figures and styling,
    so it still works after you copy it.
-   `.nojekyll` tells GitHub Pages to serve your file as it is
    (see [Turning off Jekyll with `.nojekyll`](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_521_platforms-dsci_book/lectures/quarto-github-pages.html#nojekyll)).

Copying by hand is easy to forget, so it is not how you would publish a larger site.
In DSCI 524 you will use tools that build and publish a website for you.
:::

## Submission instructions

1.  Just before you submit, create a GitHub release named something like `1.0.0`
    ([how to create a release](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/releasing-projects-on-github/managing-releases-in-a-repository#creating-a-release)).
    It records the state of your repository at submission, so you can keep working on the next milestone.
2.  On Gradescope, enter these four URLs (there is no PDF to make):
    -   your project's GitHub.com repository
    -   the GitHub release
    -   your report on GitHub Pages
    -   your image on Docker Hub

You don't need to include Milestone 1 feedback in this submission.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself before submitting

- [ ] The GitHub Actions run succeeded, and the Docker Hub tag lists `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`
- [ ] `docker-compose.yml` uses your published image with a commit-SHA tag, not `latest`
- [ ] (R) `DESCRIPTION` pins every package and lists `knitr` and `rmarkdown`
- [ ] Someone on Windows and someone on Mac followed your `README` steps exactly and rendered the report
- [ ] Your report on GitHub Pages shows in full, with its figures, and matches your release
- [ ] The GitHub Pages URL is in your `README` and in the repository's **About** section
- [ ] You created the `1.0.0` release
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Teamwork expectations (these are marked)

-   **Everyone contributes equally** to code, writing and project management,
    shown by a roughly equal number of commits, pull request reviews and GitHub issue comments.
-   Use the [GitHub flow](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/github-flow):
    a branch for each feature or fix, reviewed by at least one teammate before the pull request is merged.
-   Commit and push every time you work on the project, with meaningful commit messages
    (one or two less meaningful ones are OK).
-   Talk to your teammates in GitHub issues, not email or Slack.
-   Your question, analysis and visualization should make sense. They don't have to be complicated.
-   Write your `README` in full sentences with proper grammar. Keep point form under 10% of it.
:::
